messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Stress: Stress, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dr. Soo-Jin Park first met Mr. Kim, a 77-year-old retired surgeon of South Eastern Asian descent, in his consultation room six months after the event that had unmoored his life. Mr. Kim, a man who had spent decades commanding operating theatres with calm precision, now sat with his hands folded tightly in his lap, his eyes scanning the room in a way that suggested he was cataloguing threats rather than furniture. He had come because his wife had insisted, and because the nightmares had become unignorable, but what he wanted, he said, was for someone to explain why his own body had turned against him.

The event itself had happened in the hospital where he had worked for forty years. He had been walking through the outpatient clinic corridor when a patient, disoriented and in distress, had set himself on fire in the waiting area. Mr. Kim had not been burned. He had not been physically touched. But he had been the first physician on the scene, and he had knelt beside the man, trying to help, while the smell of burning flesh and fabric filled his nostrils. He had held the man’s hand as the flames were extinguished, and he had stayed until the code team arrived. That was the entire event, objectively speaking. But the memory did not behave like an ordinary memory. Sometimes, without warning, the full emotional horror of that moment would wash over him—the helplessness, the heat, the screaming—but there would be no image, no clear scene attached to it. He would be standing at the kitchen sink, and suddenly his chest would tighten and his throat would close, and he would have no idea why. Other times, when he did try to recall the sequence, he could not put the moments in the right order. He knew what had happened, but the timeline felt scrambled, as though someone had shuffled a deck of cards and handed him back a story that was not quite his. The memory, he told Dr. Park, felt like it belonged to someone else. He could describe it, but he did not feel connected to it.

In the months that followed, Mr. Kim had developed a set of habits that he understood, intellectually, were protective but that left him feeling increasingly trapped. He stopped watching the evening news because any mention of fires, of injuries, of emergency rooms, sent his heart racing. He stopped reading the medical journals he had once devoured, because a case report about burns or trauma could ambush him mid-page. At home, he found himself pushing away moments of genuine warmth or happiness—a laugh with his wife, the sight of his grandson’s face on a video call—because positive emotions now felt dangerous, as though letting his guard down for even a second would invite the horror back in. He tried not to think about the event at all, and for hours at a time he succeeded, but the effort was exhausting, and the thoughts always found their way back.

His body had become an unreliable witness. He startled at the sound of a car backfiring, at a door slamming, at the sudden bark of a dog. He found himself on high alert whenever he heard unexpected or loud sounds, scanning for the source, preparing for something terrible. He had also begun doing things that worried his wife: driving too fast on the freeway, taking shortcuts through unsafe neighbourhoods, ignoring his own medical checkups. He knew these were risks, but part of him no longer believed that caution mattered. What frightened him most was the conviction that his body was reacting as if he were still in danger, even when he was perfectly safe. He would be sitting in his living room, and his hands would tremble, and his breath would come short, and he would think: there is something wrong with me as a person. A surgeon does not fall apart. A surgeon stays calm. He had spent his life being the one who could handle anything, and now he could not handle a burnt smell drifting from a neighbour’s barbecue.

The trigger that undid him most often was tactile: a specific temperature on his skin. A hot shower, the warmth of a radiator, the heat rising from a cup of coffee—any of these could send him back, not to a memory, but to a feeling. And when he felt that feeling, he became convinced that he had to be especially careful, because you never knew what could happen next. He monitored doorways. He checked exits. He lived in a state of constant vigilance that his body could not switch off.

What finally brought Mr. Kim to seek help was not his own suffering but a quiet comment from his wife. She had said, one evening, that she missed him. He was physically present, she explained, but he was not really there. He had retreated into a shell of watchfulness and avoidance, and she no longer knew how to reach him. He came to Dr. Park’s office hoping to find a way back to himself, but what he feared most was that the person he had been—the steady, competent surgeon, the reliable husband, the man who could face anything—no longer existed. He was afraid that the memory that felt like it belonged to someone else had, in fact, replaced his own.
